{"id": "22:5/q16", "question": "How is ونقر read and connected syntactically?", "turns_on": "Indicative independent clause or accusative purpose; variant yāʾ and pouring-root forms.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q16/p1", "position": "The majority read indicative nuqirru, a new statement about retaining embryos.", "reasons": "Sībawayh, Farrāʾ, Zajjāj and others separate it from the purpose clause; Zajjāj argues humans were created for guidance, not simply retention; Kashf prefers coordination with 'We created.'"}, {"id": "22:5/q16/p2", "position": "An accusative/subjunctive reading coordinates retention, sometimes delivery, with 'to make clear.'", "reasons": "Transmitted from ʿĀṣim or Yaʿqūb; Zamakhsharī takes retention through birth and accountability as a second purpose; Abū al-Baqāʾ proposes an outcome lām, challenged by al-Samīn."}, {"id": "22:5/q16/p3", "position": "Third-person variants use يقر or يُقر, with indicative or accusative endings.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd, Abū Rajāʾ, Abū al-Jawzāʾ and Abū Isḥāq al-Sabīʿī are named; some yāʾ variants also govern يخرجكم."}, {"id": "22:5/q16/p4", "position": "Yaʿqūb's نَقَرُّ derives from pouring water.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, Rāzī, al-Samīn, and Ālūsī distinguish the open nūn and ḍamma on qāf from the usual retention verb."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q17", "question": "What is kept in the womb, and until when?", "turns_on": "Whether retention means avoiding miscarriage, completing formation, or fulfilling an assigned lifespan.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q17/p1", "position": "God retains selected pregnancies to completed birth rather than allowing miscarriage.", "reasons": "Mujāhid glosses completion; Ibn Zayd says stay until emergence; several sources give six months as a minimum and differing maximums. Islāḥī stresses God's choice of sex and form."}, {"id": "22:5/q17/p2", "position": "Retention lasts until the embryo completes formation.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī reports Mujāhid's gloss; some accounts tie the term to individual fetal development."}, {"id": "22:5/q17/p3", "position": "The phrase includes whoever is assigned a specified lifespan.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī offers this alternative; Ṭabarī mentions God's decree of life to a fixed term."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q18", "question": "What is the appointed term, and what gestation lengths are reported?", "turns_on": "The term is birth, but reports differ on maximum gestation.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q18/p1", "position": "The term is delivery; gestation varies, with six months often given as the minimum.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī and Bayḍāwī allow up to four years; Bursevī cites Abū Ḥanīfa's two, Shāfiʿī's four, and Mālik's five years, with anecdotes of prolonged pregnancies. Ibn ʿĀshūr says usual gestation is nine months nine days."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q19", "question": "How are ما نشاء and its pronoun read or chosen?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q19/p1", "position": "The ordinary form uses nūn with fatḥa.", "reasons": "The wording mā covers pregnancy including the inanimate morsel, as Qurṭubī notes; Biqāʿī and Islāḥī stress God's choice of which fetus continues."}, {"id": "22:5/q19/p2", "position": "Ibn Waththāb reads the nūn with kasra.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and Ālūsī transmit this vocalization."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q20", "question": "Why is طفل singular, and what does it mean?", "turns_on": "Generic or distributive singular, verbal noun, or singular licensed by the plural suffix.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q20/p1", "position": "A generic or distributive singular stands for children or each child.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda cites poetry and 66:4; al-Samīn and Rāzī allow each of you; Samarrāʾī says the verse treats the human species; the noun generally covers birth to puberty."}, {"id": "22:5/q20/p2", "position": "The singular functions as a verbal noun, applicable to one or many.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj compares ʿadl and zawr; al-Mubarrad cites 24:31; Wāḥidī discusses verbal-noun and specification parses; Ṭabarī is reported with specification."}, {"id": "22:5/q20/p3", "position": "The plural object suffix already indicates a group, making a plural predicate unnecessary.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports this distinct grammatical account; al-Suyūṭī transmits an elided distributive repetition."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q21", "question": "What are the lexical limits and related uses of طفل?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q21/p1", "position": "A tender young child, usually from birth to puberty; related roots have several senses.", "reasons": "Abū al-Haytham and Qurṭubī discuss gender and number; Qurṭubī and al-Samīn add delicate, afternoon, rain, and animal-young uses, with poetry."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q22", "question": "How does ثم لتبلغوا connect to the preceding clause?", "turns_on": "A purpose of delivery, an omitted verb, an added thumma, or a purpose tied to womb retention.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q22/p1", "position": "Reaching maturity is the purpose of bringing children out and raising them.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr defends the causal lām and rejects alternatives; Kur'an Yolu prefers causality; Ālūsī says the repeated lām emphasizes responsibility."}, {"id": "22:5/q22/p2", "position": "An omitted verb supplies 'then We let you live or grow' before the purpose clause.", "reasons": "The author of al-Naẓm, Ālūsī and Islāḥī supply the intervening development."}, {"id": "22:5/q22/p3", "position": "Thumma is additional or functions like a simple conjunction.", "reasons": "Al-Naẓm and Qurṭubī record this, comparing 39:73; Ibn ʿĀshūr instead treats thumma as marking rank or reinforcing the earlier sequence."}, {"id": "22:5/q22/p4", "position": "Maturity may be the aim of womb retention and delivery.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭībī allows this; Ālūsī rejects coordination directly with li-nubayyina as spoiling the structure."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q23", "question": "What is reaching full strength, and when does it occur?", "turns_on": "Puberty, broader complete strength, and reported numerical ages.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q23/p1", "position": "It is complete physical strength, intellect, and discernment.", "reasons": "Zajjāj sets it between thirty and forty; other sources mention eighteen, thirty-two, thirty-six, forty, forty-five. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it youth with gathered capacities."}, {"id": "22:5/q23/p2", "position": "It is the onset of puberty or sexual maturity.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā gives this gloss, and Ṭabrisī offers it as an alternative; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the verse may refer to orphan puberty."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q24", "question": "What is the grammatical form of أشد?", "turns_on": "A plural with no used singular or a plural of shiddah.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q24/p1", "position": "It is a plural-like form with no ordinary singular.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī suggests multiple aspects of strength; Nasafī repeats the form; Ālūsī surveys proposals."}, {"id": "22:5/q24/p2", "position": "It is analyzed as a plural of shiddah.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī compares anʿām from niʿmah; Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī report the analysis."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q25", "question": "When do some people die relative to maturity and old age?", "turns_on": "Before maturity, at or after maturity, or simply before senility.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q25/p1", "position": "Some die before reaching maturity.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā compares 40:67; Ibn ʿAbbās and many later commentators supply this implied timing; Islāḥī includes childhood and adolescence."}, {"id": "22:5/q25/p2", "position": "Some die before reaching decrepit old age, including at or after maturity.", "reasons": "Māwardī, Baghawī and Ṭabāṭabāʾ infer contrast with the return to old age; Rāzī specifies death at full strength; Ālūsī objects to a circumstantial parse that forces death exactly at maturity."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q26", "question": "How is يتوفى read or construed?", "turns_on": "Passive taking of life versus active completion or divine taking.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q26/p1", "position": "The usual passive form means a person is taken at death.", "reasons": "Bursevī identifies death and taking of the soul; Ālūsī says the passive leaves the understood divine agent unspoken."}, {"id": "22:5/q26/p2", "position": "An active variant takes God as subject and the person as object.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥātim transmits it; al-Samīn and Ālūsī give this parse."}, {"id": "22:5/q26/p3", "position": "An active variant takes the person as subject, meaning fulfillment of a lifespan.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās reports Abū Isḥāq; al-Samīn compares 2:234; Ālūsī records the same."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q27", "question": "What is the most decrepit age?", "turns_on": "Whether it names senility generally or a fixed age.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q27/p1", "position": "Senile old age with bodily weakness and reduced intellect; no fixed onset.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects a rigid 75-year threshold because many remain sound at eighty; Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī likewise note variation. Ṭabrisī says decline is worse than childhood weakness because childhood may improve."}, {"id": "22:5/q27/p2", "position": "It begins at a reported numerical age, seventy-five or one hundred.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya questions the report of seventy-five from ʿAlī; a report attributed to al-Ṣādiq says one hundred."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q28", "question": "What does knowing nothing after knowledge mean?", "turns_on": "Loss of past knowledge, inability to learn, loss of action, or rhetorical overstatement.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q28/p1", "position": "The elderly person forgets former knowledge and loses understanding, sometimes described emphatically as knowing nothing.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī describes repeated forgetting; Rāzī says the absolute negation intensifies loss though some knowledge remains; Islāḥī prefers that even little acquired knowledge is erased, citing 17:85."}, {"id": "22:5/q28/p2", "position": "The person can no longer acquire new knowledge and forgets what was learned.", "reasons": "Māwardī

, Ṭabrisī, Nasafī, and Abū Ḥayyān record this twofold interpretation."}, {"id": "22:5/q28/p3", "position": "The person loses the ability to act after knowing.", "reasons": "Māwardī prefers this because old age harms action more visibly than knowledge, and action depends on knowing."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q29", "question": "Are Qurʾān readers or believers spared this decline?", "turns_on": "Reports invoking 95:5–6 against Rāzī's reading of that passage.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q29/p1", "position": "Qurʾān readers, or people strengthened by faith, may be spared decrepit loss.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima and Ibn ʿAbbās cite the exception in 95:5–6; ʿAbd al-Malik says reciters retain intellect longest; Study Quran reports a faith version."}, {"id": "22:5/q29/p2", "position": "The exception in 95:5–6 concerns believers' lasting reward, not exemption from senility.", "reasons": "Rāzī rejects a literal exemption from old age, reading the return to the lowest state as blame or punishment countered by reward."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q30", "question": "What inward meanings are given to bodily decline and earth's revival?", "turns_on": "Different spiritual analogies.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q30/p1", "position": "The worst age images spiritual stagnation, veiling, desire, self-reliance, or estrangement from God.", "reasons": "Qushayrī records distinct glosses: stagnation after striving, veiling after witnessing, returning to desires, disobedience, abasement, adversaries, ignorance of one's worth, self-reliance, and illusion of independence. Baqlī adds interruption after communion."}, {"id": "22:5/q30/p2", "position": "The lifeless earth images an ignorant soul revived by knowledge and spiritual virtues.", "reasons": "Wāsiṭī says God revives humans here by knowledge and after death by spirits; Qāshānī interprets water as knowledge descending from the spirit."}, {"id": "22:5/q30/p3", "position": "Created beings emerge from the wombs of nonexistence at a divinely appointed term.", "reasons": "The Najmī inward reading transfers gestation imagery to all creation; Bursevī connects it to eternal divine will and gradual perfection."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q31", "question": "Why does the verse turn from human development to the earth?", "turns_on": "How the second sign relates to the first and why the address shifts.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q31/p1", "position": "Reviving visible dead land supplies another analogy for bodily resurrection.", "reasons": "Qushayrī invokes spring; Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts unseen origin with visible growth; Abū Ḥayyān says the second proof is directly observable; several link it to the coming Hour in 22:6–7."}, {"id": "22:5/q31/p2", "position": "The singular 'you see' invites any observer to inspect an outward sign.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī says the shift can mark a separate passage still linked by resurrection; Biqāʿī and Ālūsī address each suitable observer."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q32", "question": "What water is sent down on the earth?", "turns_on": "Rain alone or rain and other irrigation.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q32/p1", "position": "Rain is the immediate referent.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī states this; Ālūsī prefers rain because the text says it is sent down; Biqāʿī stresses its descent by divine power."}, {"id": "22:5/q32/p2", "position": "Water also includes rivers, springs, and irrigation.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān broadens the referent; Ālūsī reports that possibility."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q33", "question": "What does hāmidah describe?", "turns_on": "Dry barren land, worn-out land, dust, or literally extinguished ash.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q33/p1", "position": "Dry, lifeless, barren earth with no vegetation.", "reasons": "Lexicographers compare an extinguished fire; al-Layth adds hard crust and Shammar settled ash. Ibn ʿAbbās mentions lost moisture; al-Aʿshā's worn-clothes verse attests the root."}, {"id": "22:5/q33/p2", "position": "It means dusty, gray, or crumbling land.", "reasons": "Qatāda, Ibn Kathīr and al-Itqān specify the earth's dusty or broken appearance."}, {"id": "22:5/q33/p3", "position": "It depicts the earth literally as extinguished ash from an earlier burning state.", "reasons": "Elmalılı prefers this over summer-dried soil and invokes contemporary theories of earth as hardened deposited ash; Kur'an Yolu reports his claim."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q34", "question": "What moves when the watered earth اهتزت?", "turns_on": "The land's soil, its plants by metonymy, or an inverted event order.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q34/p1", "position": "The earth's soil stirs, loosens, or rises as vegetation sprouts.", "reasons": "Muqātil compares serpent motion in 28:31; Qurṭubī explains plant pressure metaphorically; Ibn ʿĀshūr sees upward movement; Elmalılı adds vibrating particles."}, {"id": "22:5/q34/p2", "position": "The plants move or sway; 'its vegetation' is understood.", "reasons": "Mubarrad supplies the omitted plant noun; Māwardī cites a poem about a leafy branch; Ṭabarī reports this despite the verse grammatically naming earth; Qurṭubī argues the later verb favors earth as subject."}, {"id": "22:5/q34/p3", "position": "The sense is 'swelled, then stirred' despite the verse's order.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda and Yaḥyā propose semantic inversion; Māwardī says that analysis follows the swelling-as-emergence view."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q35", "question": "What does ربت mean?", "turns_on": "Increase of earth and vegetation or swelling as plants emerge.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q35/p1", "position": "The earth swells, rises, and increases its vegetation.", "reasons": "The root r-b-w means increase; Qurṭubī unifies these senses, while Ṭabrisī and Ibn ʿĀshūr connect swelling to emerging plants. Qatāda says rain is visible in the swelling."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q36", "question": "How is وربت read?", "turns_on": "Unhamzated increase versus hamzated elevation, with differing judgments on the latter.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q36/p1", "position": "The majority read unhamzated rabat from r-b-w, 'increased or swelled.'", "reasons": "Farrāʾ and Ṭabarī reject the hamzated form as mistaken or ill-fitting; Ibn ʿAṭiyya deems it weak; other sources transmit both."}, {"id": "22:5/q36/p2", "position": "Abū Jaʿfar and others read hamzated rabaʾat, 'rose to prominence.'", "reasons": "Farrāʾ links it to a lookout but objects; Thaʿlabī cites 41:39; Qurṭubī, al-Samīn, Abū Ḥayyān, and Ibn ʿĀshūr cite the scout word and poetry."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q37", "question": "What does the earth bring forth?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q37/p1", "position": "Vegetation of many beautiful kinds and colors.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr adds varied tastes, scents, forms, and uses; Biqāʿī says paired kinds complement one another; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the beauty also grants human delight."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q38", "question": "What does zawj mean here?", "turns_on": "Species, color, or literal paired plants.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q38/p1", "position": "Each kind or species of plant.", "reasons": "Ibn Fāris allows 'variety'; Ibn ʿĀshūr derives this from the basic meaning of a paired male or female member; Biqāʿī describes complementary kinds."}, {"id": "22:5/q38/p2", "position": "Every plant color.", "reasons": "Māwardī gives green, red, and yellow; Qurṭubī allows color as a gloss."}, {"id": "22:5/q38/p3", "position": "A real pair, as opposed to a single plant.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾ offers this alternate reading and notes experimental confirmation of plant pairing."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q39", "question": "What does bahīj mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q39/p1", "position": "Beautiful, fresh, bright, and pleasing to sight or senses.", "reasons": "Qatāda gives beautiful; Mubarrad connects 27:60; Abū Zayd analyzes the adjective; al-Layth cites meadow blossoms and poetry; Ibn Qutayba notes its participial form."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q40", "question": "How do this verse's signs establish resurrection?", "turns_on": "Initial creation, repeated transformations, revived earth, and further divine attributes.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q40/p1", "position": "The One who first creates humans and revives barren earth can restore dead bodies.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Rāzī, Zamakhsharī and many others argue from initial creation to restoration; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says reason establishes possibility and revelation confirms occurrence; Islāḥī adds divine purpose and accountability."}, {"id": "22:5/q40/p2", "position": "The signs also establish God's knowledge, free will, and reality against naturalistic or reductive accounts.", "reasons": "Rāzī stresses knowledge and power, rejects reducing the resurrected person to a heart constituent; Qurṭubī says angels are only means and God alone creates; Ṭabāṭabāʾ reasons from divine truth to a lasting afterlife."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q41", "question": "What legal consequences can miscarriage or newborn signs of life have?", "turns_on": "Whether form, a recognized clot/morsel, ensoulment, cry, or another sign controls distinct rulings.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q41/p1", "position": "A recognized clot or morsel can count as delivery, ending the waiting period and sometimes establishing umm walad status.", "reasons": "Mālik and Awzāʿī accept an identifiable morsel; Qāḍī Ismāʿīl cites 65:4 and argues pregnancy existed; Qurṭubī prefers ending ʿiddah when a settled clot or morsel is expelled."}, {"id": "22:5/q41/p2", "position": "Visible human formation is required for umm walad status and, in Ibn al-ʿArabī's view, other consequences.", "reasons": "Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa accept even one discernible body part; Qurtubī reports agreement when a child is fully formed. Ibn al-ʿArabī rejects consequences before formation."}, {"id": "22:5/q41/p3", "position": "Prayer for a miscarriage requires live birth evidenced by a cry.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports the agreement on praying for a crying newborn and the view of Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, and Shāfiʿī against prayer without a cry."}, {"id": "22:5/q41/p4", "position": "Prayer may be offered for m
<<part 1 ends; continues in part 2>>

iscarriage without a cry, or after ensoulment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn al-Musayyib, and Ibn Sīrīn are named; al-Mughīra orders washing, naming and shrouding; Ibn al-ʿArabī restricts his case to a visibly formed fetus."}, {"id": "22:5/q41/p5", "position": "Inheritance and full blood money follow any certain sign of life, including movement or breathing.", "reasons": "Thawrī, Awzāʿī, and Shāfiʿī accept multiple signs; Khaṭṭābī prefers the jurists' view; Mālik requires a cry, granting only ghurra otherwise."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q42", "question": "What other reports are attached to old age in this passage?", "turns_on": "Prophetic refuge supplication versus disputed age-blessing reports.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q42/p1", "position": "The Prophet sought refuge from return to decrepit old age.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports the prayer with miserliness, cowardice, worldly trial, and grave punishment, and Saʿd says the Prophet taught it to his sons."}, {"id": "22:5/q42/p2", "position": "Reports assign successive blessings from age forty through ninety.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr records Anas and Ibn ʿUmar variants, including easier reckoning and forgiveness, but calls the raised narration extremely unusual and severely objectionable."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q43", "question": "What other grammatical and orthographic details are noted?", "turns_on": "Attachment of min, circumstantial hāmidah, joined kaylā, and min in the plant phrase.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q43/p1", "position": "Min al-baʿth attaches to rayb or qualifies it through an omitted adjective.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn states both parses; Ālūsī favors the partitive adjective analysis."}, {"id": "22:5/q43/p2", "position": "Hāmidah is an accusative circumstance of visible earth.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says tarā denotes visual perception; Ālūsī also insists on physical sight."}, {"id": "22:5/q43/p3", "position": "Li-kaylā attaches to 'is returned' and is written joined here.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn supplies the syntax; al-Nashr counts four joined occurrences; Samarrāʾī relates the joined form to immediate loss after knowledge, while Zarkashī compares parallel wording."}, {"id": "22:5/q43/p4", "position": "Min kulli zawj qualifies an omitted object, or min is extra.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports the Kufan and Akhfash allowance of extra min, leaving 'it brought forth every kind.'"}]}
{"id": "22:5/q44", "question": "What further wording choices shape the verse's argument?", "turns_on": "Specific particles, passives, word order, and direct address.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q44/p1", "position": "The wording guides the hearer through ordered stages while foregrounding the decisive sign.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr takes early thumma as real succession; Biqāʿī emphasizes passive old-age verbs and swift loss; Ālūsī says disclosure is placed first as the essential aim and maturity is marked as responsibility."}, {"id": "22:5/q44/p2", "position": "The plant scene is chosen and worded for resurrection rather than merely natural description.", "reasons": "Samarrāʾī says hāmidah suits al-Ḥajj's resurrection setting; Ibn ʿĀshūr says beautiful growth adds grace beyond the proof; Ṭabāṭabāʾ links the growth to the womb's stages."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q45", "question": "How is the verse linked to surrounding passages?", "turns_on": "Opening warnings, subsequent conclusions, and parallel creation passages.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q45/p1", "position": "It supplies proofs for the following resurrection conclusions and continues the opening warning.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls 22:6–7 a concluding tailpiece and 22:8 a return to disputants; Study Quran connects the opening's destruction and resurrection to the life cycle; Rāzī cites 36:79 and 17:51."}, {"id": "22:5/q45/p2", "position": "The verse connects with other descriptions of creation, aging, and revived earth.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī cites 23:12–13, 64:2, 40:64, 95:4 and 96:2; Study Quran lists many dead-land parallels; Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts 40:67's mention of old age."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q46", "question": "What broader sūra and Qurʾān background do these notes supply?", "turns_on": "Different sūra datings and general Qurʾān virtues.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q46/p1", "position": "Sūrat al-Ḥajj is described as Makkan, Madinan, or mixed, with a report of varied revelation settings.", "reasons": "Study Quran records the three dating views and the night/day, travel/home, war/peace report."}, {"id": "22:5/q46/p2", "position": "Qurʾān recitation and teaching receive special merit in attached reports.", "reasons": "Al-Nashr reports prophetic and later statements favoring recitation and teaching, and a dream attributed to Aḥmad about reciting with or without understanding."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q47", "question": "What ancillary linguistic examples accompany citations of this verse?", "turns_on": "Lexicographic and poetic digressions preserved in the extracted notes.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q47/p1", "position": "The sources provide additional Arabic word distinctions and poetic terminology.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba contrasts paired Arabic words and explains poetry's reliability, rhyme faults, and usage; these examples support his general lexical method rather than a separate interpretation of the verse."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q48", "question": "What other nuances do the sources give to the embryo's gradual formation?", "turns_on": "Whether the formed stage is a discrete result, an ongoing process, or one of multiple outcomes.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q48/p1", "position": "The morsel develops from the drop and clot into visible organs, with some growth incomplete.", "reasons": "Muqātil traces the formed morsel to the drop; Ibn Qutayba glosses fully formed; al-Irshād says limbs gradually become distinct.
